data.name: Blog_EYNTKAAPCA_H1_Text1
data.value: 1: Automated Hacking using AI: The Login Breach:

data.name: Blog_EYNTKAAPCA_H1_Text10
data.value: • Password Spraying

data.name: Blog_EYNTKAAPCA_H1_Text11
data.value: With brute force attacks, multiple passwords for the same ID are attempted. But this is almost useless because of the 3-strikes policy. This is where you or the attacker could get locked out of the system after 3 failed login attempts.

data.name: Blog_EYNTKAAPCA_H1_Text12
data.value: But in the event of a password spray attempt, things are a lot different and effective. Password Spraying, although a low and slow attack, attempts one common password across thousands of accounts to bypass the 3-strike policy.

data.name: Blog_EYNTKAAPCA_H1_Text13
data.value: Think of it this way.

data.name: Blog_EYNTKAAPCA_H1_Text14
data.value: Remember those helpless but annoying door-to-door self-help book salesmen?

data.name: Blog_EYNTKAAPCA_H1_Text15
data.value: Password Spraying is something along those lines, except instead of pounding on one door until the owner loses his mind and calls the cops (the three-strike policy), he rings every bell on the block with the same pitch.

data.name: Blog_EYNTKAAPCA_H1_Text16
data.value: Security ignores him cause he is not exactly harassing one person to look ‘phishy’…See what we did there?

data.name: Blog_EYNTKAAPCA_H1_Text17
data.value: Now, when we examine the Cyberverse and the world of AI-powered cyber attacks, this salesman is an autonomous agent. This agent is not looking for a ‘NO’. For this agent, ‘NO’ stands for Next Opportunity, until one of them has left their door open.

data.name: Blog_EYNTKAAPCA_H1_Text18
data.value: This slow but patient process is what allows machine learning cyber attacks breach massive networks without even alerting or alarming anyone. Humans need hours for this. An AI agent with an LLM can launch login attacks in minutes by deploying a pen-testing framework and automating the workflow.

data.name: Blog_EYNTKAAPCA_H1_Text19
data.value: 2: AI-driven cyber attacks, Ransomware and the ‘Prompt Lock’ attacks.

data.name: Blog_EYNTKAAPCA_H1_Text2
data.value: Back in the day, when someone tried to hack your login credentials, it would take days and a lot of brainwork.

data.name: Blog_EYNTKAAPCA_H1_Text20
data.value: We’re living through a wave of polymorphic, generative ransomware that is not only fast but behaves like a shapeshifter in the Cyberverse.

data.name: Blog_EYNTKAAPCA_H1_Text21
data.value: If that made your stomach drop, keep reading.

data.name: Blog_EYNTKAAPCA_H1_Text22
data.value: What started off as a research project, called Prompt Lock, is now a lucrative business model among cybercriminals. This is where basic instructions are given to an AI agent, and it can orchestrate an entire AI malware attack.

data.name: Blog_EYNTKAAPCA_H1_Text23
data.value: All of this independently without any human intervention.

data.name: Blog_EYNTKAAPCA_H1_Text24
data.value: This is the year of AI social engineering attacks, upping their ante with autonomous agents. They, i.e. the AI Agent and the LLM that are working together, are not going to strike blindly, but plan their entire mission, analyse target systems, and present the attacker with a ‘buffet’ of PII, sensitive data, even suggesting what kind of information is valuable for extortion.

data.name: Blog_EYNTKAAPCA_H1_Text25
data.value: Once the plan is set and the time is ripe, the agent launches the attacks wherein files are encrypted, malicious codes are launched, and data is exfiltrated to lock you out or threaten you with wiping out all your data.

data.name: Blog_EYNTKAAPCA_H1_Text26
data.value: These attacks can also be quite personalised. What this means is that a phishing email can be sent to you looking so convincing that you find it harmless and familiar, and that’s where the breach begins.

data.name: Blog_EYNTKAAPCA_H1_Text27
data.value: And the worst part? The code keeps changing like a shapeshifter. This makes it nearly impossible for any kind of traditional security to detect.

data.name: Blog_EYNTKAAPCA_H1_Text28
data.value: These polymorphic generative AI cyber attacks and all of the other related operations run in the cloud, which makes this a sophisticated ransomware-as-a-service cybercriminal model.

data.name: Blog_EYNTKAAPCA_H1_Text29
data.value: 3: AI phishing attacks - super personal, super intuitive for all the wrong reasons.

data.name: Blog_EYNTKAAPCA_H1_Text3
data.value: But now, Machine learning cyber attacks are the flavour of the season.

data.name: Blog_EYNTKAAPCA_H1_Text30
data.value: The good old phishing scams, now powered by AI.

data.name: Blog_EYNTKAAPCA_H1_Text31
data.value: When it comes to phishing scams, the dead giveaway is the bad grammar, weird vocabulary, terrible spelling mistakes, or just a weird feeling about it. yeah?

data.name: Blog_EYNTKAAPCA_H1_Text32
data.value: Now, imagine this: what if this comes to you in the most legitimate way possible and you actually come to believe that this is from an authentic source?

data.name: Blog_EYNTKAAPCA_H1_Text33
data.value: Okay, now here’s what happened right before you clicked that ‘Phishy’ link.

data.name: Blog_EYNTKAAPCA_H1_Text34
data.value: Phishers use LLMs from the Dark Web to generate crisp, fluent and legible emails in almost whatever language you choose.

data.name: Blog_EYNTKAAPCA_H1_Text35
data.value: That eliminates the first and loudest suspicion.

data.name: Blog_EYNTKAAPCA_H1_Text36
data.value: Now all they have to do is copy this email and paste it, and finally send it to whoever they want to attack.

data.name: Blog_EYNTKAAPCA_H1_Text37
data.value: When we speak about LLMs, we are not talking about LLMs like ChatGPT, Gemini and alike.

data.name: Blog_EYNTKAAPCA_H1_Text38
data.value: These other forms of LLMS exist on the dark web without restrictions or guardrails against malicious use and pose a serious large language model security risk.

data.name: Blog_EYNTKAAPCA_H1_Text39
data.value: The worst part about these AI phishing attacks?

data.name: Blog_EYNTKAAPCA_H1_Text4
data.value: Yes. This all began when the innocent Pen-testing framework, or the penetration testing tool that is often used to check security, fell into the hands of hackers.

data.name: Blog_EYNTKAAPCA_H1_Text40
data.value: If these attackers really want to get you, they can personalise their emails and send these AI agents to search out your social media accounts and all your presence on the internet.

data.name: Blog_EYNTKAAPCA_H1_Text41
data.value: The mail would look so hyperpersonalized that you might even gaslight yourself into believing that you actually signed up for something and forgot.

data.name: Blog_EYNTKAAPCA_H1_Text42
data.value: 4: Deepfake Cyber Threats and the Story of the 35$ Million Voice:

data.name: Blog_EYNTKAAPCA_H1_Text43
data.value: Artificial intelligence in cybercrime really brought the metaphor ‘Putting words in your mouth’ to life.

data.name: Blog_EYNTKAAPCA_H1_Text44
data.value: Yes. All these attackers need is a 3-second recording of your voice or your video. Once it is fed into the generative AI, it goes ahead and literally mimics everything about you. Now all the attacker needs to do is come up with a script.

data.name: Blog_EYNTKAAPCA_H1_Text45
data.value: And if you thought that cutting off from all your social media accounts, deleting your voice from the voicemail, and living like ‘Patrick’ under a rock could save you from deepfake cyber threats, you may want to think again.

data.name: Blog_EYNTKAAPCA_H1_Text46
data.value: In one incident of AI-driven cyber attacks in the year of 2021, according to IBM, there was an audio deepfake that was executed.

data.name: Blog_EYNTKAAPCA_H1_Text47
data.value: In this deepfake cyber threats incident, the attacker, reportedly impersonating their boss, asked the employee to wire them 35 million dollars to a particular account. Guess what?

data.name: Blog_EYNTKAAPCA_H1_Text48
data.value: The naive and clueless employee believed the attacker and the company lost 35 million dollars, just like that.

data.name: Blog_EYNTKAAPCA_H1_Text49
data.value: AI phishing attacks have been evolving, and in 2024, an attacker attempted a deepfake video and simulated a video pretending to be a CFO of the company and convinced an employee to wire 25 million dollars to the fraudster.

data.name: Blog_EYNTKAAPCA_H1_Text5
data.value: What was initially used by ethical hackers to test security is now being deployed by hackers and attackers to brute force their way into your systems.

data.name: Blog_EYNTKAAPCA_H1_Text50
data.value: Remember the saying, “Seeing is believing” Now, the future of cyber security 2026, seeing is not enough unless they are present in person.

data.name: Blog_EYNTKAAPCA_H1_Text51
data.value: 5: AI-driven cyber attacks, The CVE Genie and its Autonomous Hacking Tools:

data.name: Blog_EYNTKAAPCA_H1_Text52
data.value: This is a prime example of how the weakest cog in the wheel can overturn the whole vehicle. Except in the security industry, these exploits are published, and they are called Common Vulnerabilities and Exposures.

data.name: Blog_EYNTKAAPCA_H1_Text53
data.value: These publications or reports are written by security experts who identify major vulnerabilities, describe them, number them, document them, and catalogue them, and this information is publicly available.

data.name: Blog_EYNTKAAPCA_H1_Text54
data.value: This is another research project that welcomed the darkness, and unfortunately, autonomous hacking tools have turned this public safety data into a weapon. Attackers took the data and information of this CVE and used an AI agent to develop a CVE genie.

data.name: Blog_EYNTKAAPCA_H1_Text55
data.value: Now, what this agent did is, it fed the CVE data to the LLM, which went through all the problem statements, pulled out the salient details and then came up with a plan and then sent this bundle of information back to the genie.

data.name: Blog_EYNTKAAPCA_H1_Text56
data.value: This genie then processes all of the vulnerabilities and then devises the exploit code for the attackers.

data.name: Blog_EYNTKAAPCA_H1_Text57
data.value: This was pretty much 51% sucessful, and you know what this means for AI-driven cyber attacks?

data.name: Blog_EYNTKAAPCA_H1_Text58
data.value: It means that anyone with a bare minimum understanding of how coding works can easily use this information and deploy an AI agent at their disposal to exploit systems.

data.name: Blog_EYNTKAAPCA_H1_Text59
data.value: This costs less than $3 (the price of a pack of Kool-Aid), and this lowers the barrier to entry so significantly that anyone with basic coding knowledge can launch high-level AI-powered cyber attacks.

data.name: Blog_EYNTKAAPCA_H1_Text6
data.value: Attackers deploy autonomous AI agents paired with an LLM. The two of them work in tandem, where the AI agent gets the job done, and the LLM supports the AI agent with the necessary information.

data.name: Blog_EYNTKAAPCA_H1_Text60
data.value: 6: AI-driven cyber attacks - The Final Boss or the kill chain:

data.name: Blog_EYNTKAAPCA_H1_Text61
data.value: Meet the final boss of Artificial Intelligence in cybercrime - the fully automated kill chain.

data.name: Blog_EYNTKAAPCA_H1_Text62
data.value: If you thought that is yet to happen, it is already in action as you read this article.

data.name: Blog_EYNTKAAPCA_H1_Text63
data.value: These particular AI-driven cyber attacks are notoriously leveraging systems like Anthropic to execute brutal operations.

data.name: Blog_EYNTKAAPCA_H1_Text64
data.value: In these forms of attacks, the AI agent behaves like a master strategist, and conducts independent research on identifying high-value targets, analyses sensitive data and even designs fake personas to hide any kind of trails or breadcrumbs.

data.name: Blog_EYNTKAAPCA_H1_Text65
data.value: These agents enhance the AI-driven cyber attacks by also taking strong economic decisions for you, by thoroughly analysing the victim’s financial worth, the assets they hold, and finally calibrating the ransom they can demand to ensure they are just enough to be fruitful and low enough for the victim to be compelled to pay.

data.name: Blog_EYNTKAAPCA_H1_Text66
data.value: And you thought your ex was good at manipulating you?

data.name: Blog_EYNTKAAPCA_H1_Text7
data.value: And this is where it gets interesting, these AI-driven cyber attacks are spearheaded by these AI agents that identify login pages and instantly parse HTML for credential fields, login forms and try to capture IDs, passwords, and OTPs.

data.name: Blog_EYNTKAAPCA_H1_Text8
data.value: Now that the information is gathered, there are two major ways the attacks are conducted;

data.name: Blog_EYNTKAAPCA_H1_Text9
data.value: • Brute Force Attacks

data.name: Blog_EYNTKAAPCA_H2_Text1
data.value: On the contrary, the future of cybersecurity in 2026 is at risk, and we have moved past the point of traditional firewalls and antiviruses as ‘just enough’ protection.

data.name: Blog_EYNTKAAPCA_H2_Text2
data.value: As AI-driven cyber attacks become creative and more autonomous, polymorphic, and economically savvy, the gap between ‘elite hackers’ and ‘vide coders’ is closing.

data.name: Blog_EYNTKAAPCA_H2_Text3
data.value: We are witnessing a massive shift in cyberattacks where artificial intelligence in cybercrime and the speed it takes to attack outpace human reaction time.

data.name: Blog_EYNTKAAPCA_H2_Text4
data.value: However, this is not a lost battle. It’s time to think like a hacker to beat the hacker, but with better tech and understanding.

data.name: Blog_EYNTKAAPCA_Heading1
data.value: If you’re still reading this, here are the 6 most dangerous AI-driven cyber attacks and methods currently being deployed.

data.value: Well, Arnie tried to warn us, and as we cosy up to 2026, the warnings are becoming a reality, and fiction is now becoming a fact.

data.name: Blog_EYNTKAAPCA_Text3

data.name: Blog_EYNTKAAPCA_Text4

data.name: Blog_EYNTKACSE_H1_Text8

data.name: Blog_FILUTPDADBAAAATH_H1_Text1
data.value: The IVY league university is home to 20,000 faculty and staff, 24,500 students in both undergraduate and postgraduate programs, and 400,000 alumni around the world.

data.name: Blog_FILUTPDADBAAAATH_H1_Text10
data.value: Harvard managed to block any further access to prevent any kind of unauthorised activity, and they have turned to a third-party cybersecurity partner and law enforcement to prevent any further incidents.

data.name: Blog_FILUTPDADBAAAATH_H1_Text2
data.value: With Harvard, databases of alumni, donors, students and faculty records were breached.

data.name: Blog_FILUTPDADBAAAATH_H1_Text3
data.value: This screams one loud message, and that is: these hackers are not just trying to tap into financial data, but they want identities, networks, influence, leverage, and details of important student profiles.

data.name: Blog_FILUTPDADBAAAATH_H1_Text4
data.value: Universities and other forms of educational institutions carry a wealth of information when it comes to personal histories, notable alumni details, and family networks, and that is just the personal part of it.

data.name: Blog_FILUTPDADBAAAATH_H1_Text5
data.value: As for the actual price, these institutions are a goldmine of datasets carrying information regarding research documents, experimental outcomes, grant records and communications, academic archives, and other highly confidential internal communications and information.

data.name: Blog_FILUTPDADBAAAATH_H1_Text6
data.value: • What was exposed?

data.name: Blog_FILUTPDADBAAAATH_H1_Text7
data.value: The breach exposed contact details, biographical data, email addresses, phone numbers, home and business addresses, and other sensitive information. The breach also included details of the alumni spouses, contact details for current students and parents.

data.name: Blog_FILUTPDADBAAAATH_H1_Text8
data.value: Financial records, passwords and SSN were not leaked, but information about donations, gifts, information related to fundraising and alumni engagement activities where exposed.

data.name: Blog_FILUTPDADBAAAATH_H1_Text9
data.value: • The University’s response to the attack:

data.name: Blog_FILUTPDADBAAAATH_H2_Text1
data.value: While Harvard was attacked twice in the same year, other Ivy League universities, such as the University of Pennsylvania and Princeton, also faced similar breaches.

data.name: Blog_FILUTPDADBAAAATH_H2_Text10
data.value: • The Princeton database breach occurred on November 10th, and this was also a phone phishing attack.

data.name: Blog_FILUTPDADBAAAATH_H2_Text11
data.value: • Although the breach was for less than 24 hours, it had a lasting impact. This is because the breach exposed information about fundraising activities and donations.

data.name: Blog_FILUTPDADBAAAATH_H2_Text12
data.value: • Sources say that the attack put nearly 100,000 people’s personal information at risk.

data.name: Blog_FILUTPDADBAAAATH_H2_Text13
data.value: • According to other sources, one of them claims that the hackers have taken sufficient and more information to commit identity theft and wreak havoc on thousands of individuals.

data.name: Blog_FILUTPDADBAAAATH_H2_Text14
data.value: • The investigation may take several weeks to examine what data was exactly compromised.

data.name: Blog_FILUTPDADBAAAATH_H2_Text15
data.value: The University’s response to the attack:

data.name: Blog_FILUTPDADBAAAATH_H2_Text16
data.value: • The attack was ceased within 24 hours.

data.name: Blog_FILUTPDADBAAAATH_H2_Text17
data.value: • An external set of cybersecurity experts was deployed, and the law and order systems were notified, too.

data.name: Blog_FILUTPDADBAAAATH_H2_Text18
data.value: • Princeton also notified the community about being vigilant of phishing attacks and which also enhanced their security protocols and training.

data.name: Blog_FILUTPDADBAAAATH_H2_Text2
data.value: The University of Pennsylvania Data Breach:

data.name: Blog_FILUTPDADBAAAATH_H2_Text3
data.value: • The breach happened on the 30th of October. The threat actors used an employee’s PennKey SSO account to breach the university’s Salesforce instance, Qlik analytics platform, SAP business intelligence systems, and SharePoint files.

data.name: Blog_FILUTPDADBAAAATH_H2_Text4
data.value: • Hackers stole 1.71 GB of internal documents from the SharePoint and Box Storage platforms, which consisted of documents, financial information and alumni marketing materials.

data.name: Blog_FILUTPDADBAAAATH_H2_Text5
data.value: • Another claim in the digital heist is that they could’ve stolen nearly 1.2 million records of PII, including donation history and other demographic details.

data.name: Blog_FILUTPDADBAAAATH_H2_Text6
data.value: • The hackers also sent out mass emails from Penn.edu, which not only consisted of offensive emails, but also exposed tens of thousands of internal university files on online forums.

data.name: Blog_FILUTPDADBAAAATH_H2_Text7
data.value: The University’s response to the attack:

data.name: Blog_FILUTPDADBAAAATH_H2_Text8
data.value: The infected systems were promptly locked down to stop further intrusion or any kind of unauthorised access. They turned to a third-party cybersecurity firm, CrowdStrike, to investigate the incident. Penn further reported this incident to the FBI and has now also implemented the necessary security patches issued by Oracle to resolve the exploited vulnerabilities.

data.name: Blog_FILUTPDADBAAAATH_H2_Text9
data.value: The Princeton Breach:

data.name: Blog_FILUTPDADBAAAATH_H3_Text1
data.value: Well, this year’s breach can be next year’s impersonator.

data.name: Blog_FILUTPDADBAAAATH_H3_Text2
data.value: It is never about what they possess; it is always about what they could do with all that data. It's about how they use that to build something dangerous tomorrow.

data.name: Blog_FILUTPDADBAAAATH_H3_Text3
data.value: Stolen data can either be sold or held for ransom, and that is just skimming on the surface level of what could actually unfold.

data.name: Blog_FILUTPDADBAAAATH_H3_Text4
data.value: When a hacker attacks an educational institution, they are not looking at just siphoning out data. They want leverage. They steal data because it is a multi-use asset. That data can be used, sold, used for impersonation, held as ransom or even worse, weaponised and automated.

data.name: Blog_FILUTPDADBAAAATH_H3_Text5
data.value: With universities in focus, especially Ivy League universities, the student and faculty data that is exploited is of high value. And this is because these students or faculty are not mere regular individuals. The data also consists of information about donors, alumni, professors, researchers, and donors who come with high social and financial capital.

data.name: Blog_FILUTPDADBAAAATH_H3_Text6
data.value: Today, a single phishing email, or an email containing some enticing information, could expose your entire bank account, be it a business account, personal or a joint account. This could even manipulate your login request, or even go on to hijack digital identities tomorrow.

data.name: Blog_FILUTPDADBAAAATH_H3_Text7
data.value: And that is precisely why encryption is important.

data.name: Blog_FILUTPDADBAAAATH_H3_Text8
data.value: With encryption, even if a breach happens, at most, they only see your files, but they can never open them and alter the information.

data.name: Blog_FILUTPDADBAAAATH_H4_Text1
data.value: Once academic data or any data for that matter is exposed or compromised, it is then taken hostage to cyber marketplaces where it is either sold, copied, multiplied, duplicated indefinitely. This means leaked data is never truly gone.

data.name: Blog_FILUTPDADBAAAATH_H4_Text2
data.value: While it seems absolutely harmless, this is just cannon fodder for targeted cybercrimes and personalised harassment. The real fun for hackers is that it is not just raw data that they are playing with. They are playing around with the credibility attached to it.

data.name: Blog_FILUTPDADBAAAATH_H4_Text3
data.value: With university-based data breaches, attackers are impersonating trusted people in the university’s system to make phishing attempts and use socially enriched tactics to look super convincing.

data.name: Blog_FILUTPDADBAAAATH_H4_Text4
data.value: Through this, in the end, the greatest risk is not exposure of information. It is using trust as a weapon, familiarity as a perfect loophole, using connection to manipulate access, finances, and using a simple professional relationship that is familiar to an insider to take complete control.

data.name: Blog_FILUTPDADBAAAATH_H4_Text5
data.value: All of this and more under the guise of a legitimate academic connection.

data.name: Blog_FILUTPDADBAAAATH_H5_Text1
data.value: Encryption is no longer an option, and it is most definitely not a fire drill that happens once in a while. It needs to be a daily practice among organisations to prevent serious breaches.

data.name: Blog_FILUTPDADBAAAATH_H5_Text2
data.value: Be it encryption for business or just for personal use, it is an investment in your peace of mind and a perfect protection for your identity.

data.name: Blog_FILUTPDADBAAAATH_H5_Text3
data.value: • How encryption works.

data.name: Blog_FILUTPDADBAAAATH_H5_Text4
data.value: Encryption, if implemented properly, basically means even if someone were to access your device or drive, they will be left with nothing but unreadable and useless ciphertext. For instance, the AES-256-bit encryption is one of the strongest, unbeatable and trusted types of encryption present. And the best part? AxCrypt offers you this, along with layered security like password protection and data breach prevention.

data.name: Blog_FILUTPDADBAAAATH_H5_Text5
data.value: Whether you want secure file sharing options for documents like your property papers, legal documents, research material, and other documents, this encryption is a silent but loud shield protecting your privacy and peace of mind.

data.name: Blog_FILUTPDADBAAAATH_H6_Text1
data.value: Not all attacks need to be a digital loophole. Some just need a gullible person on the team or a familiar voice that is on the other end of the line.

data.name: Blog_FILUTPDADBAAAATH_H6_Text10
data.value: Now this is only merely an example of how your instincts, along with a zero-knowledge encryption software, could save you from being the next breach headline.

data.name: Blog_FILUTPDADBAAAATH_H6_Text2
data.value: Here is a simple rule to spot a vishing attack from taking over you.

data.name: Blog_FILUTPDADBAAAATH_H6_Text3
data.value: Got a random call at work? Seems quite familiar, but something seems off? Just verify that call with a simple, harmless, and personal question that only you and the other person who is being impersonated know.

data.name: Blog_FILUTPDADBAAAATH_H6_Text4
data.value: For example...

data.name: Blog_FILUTPDADBAAAATH_H6_Text5
data.value: Impersonator pretending to be Mr David: Hey Jane… I need you to open my laptop and send me the “ABC” file immediately.

data.name: Blog_FILUTPDADBAAAATH_H6_Text6
data.value: This is EXACTLY where the breach unfolds.

data.name: Blog_FILUTPDADBAAAATH_H6_Text7
data.value: Either Jane, from accounts, can give the impersonator the file and get the company bankrupt, OR she can prevent a Vishing attack and get promoted with a really good hike for this move she pulled.

data.name: Blog_FILUTPDADBAAAATH_H6_Text8
data.value: Jane: Sure. I’ll do that. But hey, how did your dentist appointment go? Did they remove the tooth?

data.name: Blog_FILUTPDADBAAAATH_H6_Text9
data.value: Now the impersonator will answer, just to play along until they get their hands on what they are looking for. But Jane is smarter. She hangs up immediately and informs Mr David, who is on vacation in Bora Bora with his family.

data.name: Blog_FILUTPDADBAAAATH_Summary
data.value: The IVY league university is home to 20,000 faculty and staff, 24,500 students in both undergraduate and postgraduate programs, and 400,000 alumni around the world.With Harvard, databases of alumni, donors, students and faculty records were breached.This screams one loud message, and that is: these hackers are not just trying to tap into financial data, but they want identities, networks, influence, leverage, and details of important student profiles.

data.name: Blog_FILUTPDADBAAAATH_Text1
data.value: It took nothing more than a phone call with a familiar and convincing voice, a malicious actor impersonating as an internal contact, and just the right insider on the other end of the line. This is how a skilled hacker got their ‘Vish’.

data.name: Blog_FILUTPDADBAAAATH_Text2
data.value: Meet the brand new cybercriminal business model, ‘Vishing’.

data.name: Blog_FILUTPDADBAAAATH_Text3
data.value: The act of impersonating a familiar entity to garner pity or fear or even sympathy to gain critical information like bank account numbers, OTPs, passwords and more.

data.name: Blog_FILUTPDADBAAAATH_Text4
data.value: Hackers and attackers are upgrading to this convincing scam as a form of weaponised persuasion.

data.name: Blog_FILUTPDADBAAAATH_Text5
data.value: Familiarity – a psychological loophole that easily cuts through firewalls, BitLocker, antiviruses and sinks its claws deep into naive human trust. This is the beginning of all breaches, scams and ransom attacks. Because familiarity cements trust, and digital trust translates into something like ‘I know this person…let me give them what they are asking for’.

data.name: Blog_FILUTPDADBAAAATH_Text6
data.value: The more familiar your digital interactions become, the less suspicious you become, and that is exactly the kind of treats that these attackers feast on.

data.name: Blog_FILUTPDADBAAAATH_Text7
data.value: In this article, we will dive into how an elite university was prey to something as simple as a phone call with a familiar voice on the other end of the line.

data.name: Blog_FOKM_H1_Text1
data.value: Effective data security is built on the foundation of key management also known as KMS. It is the process of administering or managing cryptographic keys. A critical feature of any KMS is its capacity to handle keys systematically throughout its lifecycle: key generation, key import/export, key distribution, key usage, key update, key backup, key revocation, and key deletion. Data is encrypted and decrypted using encryption keys, therefore the loss or compromise of any encryption key renders the data protection. It also ensures the safe transmission of data across an internet connection and not just includes access control but also monitoring and logging of each key's access, use, and context.

data.name: Blog_FOKM_H2_Text1
data.value: Key management deals with numerous types of security risks beyond encryption, such as people and incorrect policies, cyber attacks and data theft on networks. It is one of the most difficult components of cryptography. It also entails developing a system policy, user training, interdepartmental collaboration, and effective coordination.

data.name: Blog_FOKM_H2_Text2
data.value: In large corporations all members have access to the company data, therefore security is a major concern. The solution is a multicast group key management system that securely distributes individual keys to each member. In this way, material encrypted with a single group member's key can only be accessed and read by that group member.

data.name: Blog_FOKM_H2_Text3
data.value: Key Management also includes controls to guarantee that keys are only accessible to authorised personnel and systems, that they are only used for their intended purposes, and that all key activities are logged for audit and compliance purposes.

data.name: Blog_FOKM_H3_SH3_Text1
data.value: Key sharing is a feature that allows you to keep your data secure while also sharing it with your colleagues. It enables you to collaborate and connect with other members without jeopardising the confidentiality of your data. Using AxCrypt's key sharing function you can give anyone data access and withdraw it whenever you want; you don't even have to disclose your own password. With their own password, the other user can access the shared files. For more info on AxCrypt key sharing check our key sharing tutorial on You Tube for a better understanding of AxCrypt's key sharing capability.

data.name: Blog_FOKM_H3_SH4_Text1
data.value: Master Key is highly secure, it can be viewed as an automatic sharing of files with the administrators of the business. data.name: Blog_FWC2CTWFLEPSD_H1_Text1
data.value: Imagine a World Cup ticket lands in your inbox with a QR code and a registration link. It looks real, so you enter your details, and just like that, your payment information, login credentials, and personal data are in the wrong hands.

data.name: Blog_FWC2CTWFLEPSD_H1_Text2
data.value: A few years ago, scams were easier to spot: badly written emails, strange addresses, clumsy designs. Not anymore. Cybercriminals now use AI to create polished websites, deepfake videos, fake audio, and convincing phishing messages that mimic legitimate organisations. Technology can help detect threats, but fans still need to stay alert.

data.name: Blog_FWC2CTWFLEPSD_H1_Text3
data.value: Here are some of the ways cybercriminals are exploiting fans around the world.

data.name: Blog_FWC2CTWFLEPSD_H1_Text4
data.value: • Fake FIFA tickets and hospitality scams remain one of the biggest threats.

data.name: Blog_FWC2CTWFLEPSD_H1_Text5
data.value: • World Cup phishing scams arrive via email, text, or social media.

data.name: Blog_FWC2CTWFLEPSD_H1_Text6
data.value: • Travel scams FIFA World Cup fans often face include fake hotel bookings.

data.name: Blog_FWC2CTWFLEPSD_H1_Text7
data.value: • World Cup streaming scams involve malicious apps promising free live matches.

data.name: Blog_FWC2CTWFLEPSD_H1_Text8
data.value: • World Cup social media scams spread rapidly through fake accounts.

data.name: Blog_FWC2CTWFLEPSD_H2_Text1
data.value: One of the most effective ways to protect yourself is learning how to identify fake websites quickly. Here's what to look for:

data.name: Blog_FWC2CTWFLEPSD_H2_Text2
data.value: • Beware of typosquatting: This scam mimics the original website's URL or slug with a minor spelling mistake. For example, instead of https://www.fifa.com/en, the word 'FIFA' in the URL may include an extra letter. Users click this hastily because it looks familiar, then get redirected to the attacker's site, where they willingly give up their credentials because the site seems authentic. Read more in this article: What is Typosquatting & How Does Encryption Protect Your Data?

data.name: Blog_FWC2CTWFLEPSD_H2_Text3
data.value: • Look for HTTPS and the padlock icon: Legitimate sites use secure HTTPS connections. However, having HTTPS alone does not guarantee the site is safe.

data.name: Blog_FWC2CTWFLEPSD_H2_Text4
data.value: • Keep an eye out for suspicious, poor and unorganised design: Fake websites try really hard to look legit. Low-quality images, spelling mistakes like a toddler wrote the content, broken links, unprofessional layouts, links that automatically redirect you to other sites, etc., are all signs of an attacker or scam website.

data.name: Blog_FWC2CTWFLEPSD_H2_Text5
data.value: • Lack of proper contact information: Genuine sites provide clear contact details, physical addresses, and customer support. Be wary of sites with only a contact form.

data.name: Blog_FWC2CTWFLEPSD_H2_Text6
data.value: • Unwanted pressure tactics: Fake websites often use pressure tactics. They display unrealistic offers, passive-aggressive discount prompts, and phrases like 'only 2 tickets left!' to rush you into signing up and revealing your details.

data.name: Blog_FWC2CTWFLEPSD_H2_Text7
data.value: If websites are not the only ones that are scamming people this FIFA World Cup season, scammers, attackers and the like have levelled up with fake tickets too.

data.name: Blog_FWC2CTWFLEPSD_H3_SH1_Text1
data.value: • Fake sender name: The email claims to come from 'Official FIFA Tickets'. Real FIFA communications always use official domains like @fifa.com or @tickets.fifa.com. This one uses a generic or spoofed address.

data.name: Blog_FWC2CTWFLEPSD_H3_SH1_Text10
data.value: • Do not share any personal or payment information.

data.name: Blog_FWC2CTWFLEPSD_H3_SH1_Text11
data.value: • Mark the email as spam and delete it.

data.name: Blog_FWC2CTWFLEPSD_H3_SH1_Text12
data.value: • Only buy or manage tickets through the official FIFA website (http://fifa.com/tickets) or the official FWC2026 Mobile Tickets app.

data.name: Blog_FWC2CTWFLEPSD_H3_SH1_Text13
data.value: Scammers target fans during the FIFA World Cup 2026. Stay alert and verify all communications through official channels to protect yourself.

data.name: Blog_FWC2CTWFLEPSD_H3_SH1_Text2
data.value: • Suspicious link: The link (www.fifa-ticket-access2026.com) is not an official FIFA site. Scammers create lookalike domains to steal personal and payment details.

data.name: Blog_FWC2CTWFLEPSD_H3_SH1_Text3
data.value: • Unusual payment methods: The email requests payment via cryptocurrency, wire transfer, or gift cards. FIFA accepts payments only through secure, recognised gateways on its official platform. Legitimate organisations never ask for cryptocurrency or gift cards for tickets.

data.name: Blog_FWC2CTWFLEPSD_H3_SH1_Text4
data.value: • High-pressure tactics: Phrases like 'complete payment within the next 2 hours' and 'availability is limited' aim to create panic and prevent clear thinking. Real FIFA ticket sales do not operate this way.

data.name: Blog_FWC2CTWFLEPSD_H3_SH1_Text5
data.value: • Fake exclusivity claim: FIFA runs ticket sales phases and resale options but never sends random 'exclusive early access' emails like this. Official information comes only through verified channels and your FIFA account.

data.name: Blog_FWC2CTWFLEPSD_Text1
data.value: As the world witnesses Cristiano Ronaldo making history by becoming the first player to score in a record six FIFA World Cups and South Africa reaching the knockout stages for the first time ever, the excitement around this year's FIFA World Cup has certainly reached a fever pitch.

data.name: Blog_FWC2CTWFLEPSD_Text2
data.value: With all the merriment across all the host cities like Canada, the United States and Mexico and the dramatic goals, the tournament is sure to be delivering unforgettable moments. And while the world's vision is focused on this, cybercriminals have upped their ante and are coming in strong with dangerous scams.

data.name: Blog_FWC2CTWFLEPSD_Text3
data.value: FIFA World Cup 2026 scams are seeing a significant rise, and sources claim that there are over 13,000 new FIFA-themed domains registered in the first five months of 2026 alone, with thousands more flagged as suspicious or malicious.

data.name: Blog_FWC2CTWFLEPSD_Text4
data.value: Needless to say, this global event is one of the easiest targets that cybercriminals can leverage to exploit fans and other football fanatics. According to a report by The Hacker News, nearly 6 million fans are expected across the United States, Canada and Mexico, and it is said to receive more than 150 million ticket requests in the first 15 days, which leaves the tournament 30 times oversubscribed.

data.name: Blog_FWC2CTWFLEPSD_Text5
data.value: The scarcity of tickets; anxious fans desperate for discounts and a chance to see Messi on the field live in action; and money moving faster than the speed of light – these are ground zero for cybercriminals, hackers and attackers.

data.name: Blog_FWC2CTWFLEPSD_Text6
data.value: FIFA World Cup 2026 scams are seeing an all-time rise thanks to fake tickets, phishing messages and fraudulent travel offers. The rise is not just because of cybercriminals maximising this event; it's the sheer nature of these scams looking absolutely legitimate at first glance, making it convincing for fans to give up their details, just like that.

data.name: Blog_FWC2CTWFLEPSD_Text7
data.value: From World Cup streaming scams to World Cup phishing scams to travel and accommodation scams, this article will give you an insight into what you must watch out for this FIFA season.

data.name: Blog_GAES256BEWA_H1_Text1
data.value: The National Institute of Standards and Technology (NIST) recognized the need for an alternative to the Data Encryption Standard (DES), which was becoming vulnerable to brute-force attacks, and thus Advanced Encryption Standard (AES) was created. The US National Security Agency (NSA) authorized AES as the first publicly available cipher for protecting top-secret material.Learn More

data.name: Blog_GAES256BEWA_H1_Text2
data.value: Cybercriminals are constantly on the lookout for weak points to exploit. How can users have complete confidence that their data is safe, no matter where it is stored, especially in this increasingly connected world? Encryption is one of the most prevalent methods for safeguarding sensitive information. Encryption works by turning ordinary text to ciphertext, which consists of seemingly random characters. It can only be decrypted by those who hold the unique key.

data.name: Blog_GAES256BEWA_Heading1
data.value: Why is AES 256-bit encryption required?

data.name: Blog_GAES256BEWA_Summary
data.value: AES is a symmetric algorithm, meaning it uses the same key for encryption and decryption. The technique has been built to accommodate key sizes of 128, 192, and 256 bits.

data.name: Blog_GAES256BEWA_Text1
data.value: AES is a symmetric algorithm, meaning it uses the same key for encryption and decryption. The technique has been built to accommodate key sizes of 128, 192, and 256 bits. It is known as the strongest and most robust encryption standard commercially available today.

data.name: Blog_GAES256BEWA_Text2
data.value: AES-256 bit encryption has a key length of 256 bits and supports the greatest bit size and is practically unbreakable by brute force based on existing computing capability. A brute-force attack is when a hacker checks all possible key combinations until the correct key is found.Learn More

data.name: Blog_HAESGC_H1_Text1
data.value: GDPR is a set of regulations designed to protect personal data and ensure that businesses handle this data responsibly. It emphasizes transparency, security, and accountability in how personal data is processed and stored. As of 2024, fines for GDPR non-compliance have reached significant levels, with some organizations facing millions of euros in penalties.

data.name: Blog_HAESGC_H1_Text2
data.value: GDPR compliance requires businesses to take specific actions to protect personal data, including securing it against unauthorized access, ensuring transparency with individuals, and offering them control over their data. This is where AxCrypt, with its robust GDPR encryption software, becomes an essential tool for safeguarding sensitive information.

data.name: Blog_HAESGC_H2_Text1
data.value: 1. Lawfulness, Fairness, and Transparency:

data.name: Blog_HAESGC_H2_Text10
data.value: Personal data must be adequate, relevant, and limited to what is necessary. According to Article 5(1)(c):

data.name: Blog_HAESGC_H2_Text11
data.value: Adequate, relevant and limited to what is necessary in relation to the purposes for which they are processed (‘data minimization’).

data.name: Blog_HAESGC_H2_Text12
data.value: AxCrypt allows businesses to encrypt only the data that is essential, helping with GDPR’s data minimization principle. Instead of storing large volumes of unprotected data, businesses can choose to encrypt only the most critical files, reducing the risk of unnecessary data processing.

data.name: Blog_HAESGC_H2_Text13
data.value: 4. Integrity and Confidentiality:

data.name: Blog_HAESGC_H2_Text14
data.value: Perhaps the most relevant feature of AxCrypt in the context of GDPR compliance software is its encryption capabilities. Article 5(1)(f) states:

data.name: Blog_HAESGC_H2_Text15
data.value: Processed in a manner that ensures appropriate security of the personal data, including protection against unauthorized or unlawful processing and against accidental loss, destruction or damage, using appropriate technical or organisational measures (‘integrity and confidentiality’).

data.name: Blog_HAESGC_H2_Text16
data.value: Data must be kept secure against unauthorized access, accidental loss, or destruction. AxCrypt’s GDPR file encryption software ensures that only authorized users can decrypt and access files, maintaining confidentiality and integrity as required by GDPR compliance standards.

data.name: Blog_HAESGC_H2_Text2
data.value: Under GDPR regulations, businesses must process personal data in a lawful, fair, and transparent manner. As stated in Article 5(1)(a):

data.name: Blog_HAESGC_H2_Text3
data.value: Personal data shall be processed lawfully, fairly and in a transparent manner in relation to the data subject (‘lawfulness, fairness and transparency’).

data.name: Blog_HAESGC_H2_Text4
data.value: This includes clearly informing individuals about how their data will be used. With AxCrypt, businesses can encrypt sensitive personal data, ensuring that even if unauthorized individuals access it, they cannot read or misuse it. This contributes to secure GDPR compliance through GDPR data protection encryption.

data.name: Blog_HAESGC_H2_Text5
data.value: 2. Purpose Limitation:

data.name: Blog_HAESGC_H2_Text6
data.value: GDPR mandates that personal data should only be collected for specific, explicit, and legitimate purposes. Article 5(1)(b) states:

data.name: Blog_HAESGC_H2_Text7
data.value: Collected for specified, explicit and legitimate purposes and not further processed in a manner that is incompatible with those purposes (‘purpose limitation’).

data.name: Blog_HAESGC_H2_Text8
data.value: AxCrypt ensures that businesses store only necessary data and that it remains protected, helping organizations comply with the GDPR purpose limitation principle by preventing unnecessary exposure of personal data.

data.name: Blog_HAESGC_H2_Text9
data.value: 3. Data Minimization:

data.name: Blog_HAESGC_H3_Text1
data.value: GDPR grants individuals several rights, including:

data.name: Blog_HAESGC_H3_Text2
data.value: • Right to Access: Individuals can request access to their personal data. With AxCrypt, organizations can easily retrieve and decrypt files to fulfill these requests.

data.name: Blog_HAESGC_H3_Text3
data.value: • Right to Rectification: AxCrypt allows businesses to encrypt the most up-to-date data, ensuring accuracy while maintaining data integrity.

data.name: Blog_HAESGC_H3_Text4
data.value: • Right to Erasure (“ Right to be Forgotten”): AxCrypt offers a reliable solution for ensuring secure deletion of files. When businesses need to erase personal data, they can securely decrypt and delete files, fully complying with this GDPR right.

data.name: Blog_HAESGC_H3_Text5
data.value: Data Protection by Design and Default

data.name: Blog_HAESGC_H3_Text6
data.value: One of GDPR's core principles is that organizations must incorporate data protection into the design of their systems and processes. This is known as “data protection by design and by default.” By using AxCrypt GDPR features, businesses are embedding robust GDPR data security into their daily operations, ensuring GDPR compliance from the outset.

data.name: Blog_HAESGC_H4_Text1
data.value: 1. Encryption for Security and Privacy: AxCrypt employs AES-256 encryption, widely regarded as one of the most secure encryption methods available today. By encrypting data at rest, in transit, and during processing, businesses ensure that sensitive data remains secure at all times, reducing the likelihood of unauthorized access or GDPR breaches.

data.name: Blog_HAESGC_H4_Text2
data.value: 2. Simplified Consent Management: While AxCrypt doesn't handle consent management directly, it plays a critical role in ensuring that any consent-related data remains protected. By using GDPR encryption software, businesses can guarantee that any personal information or consent records are securely stored and only accessible to authorized personnel.

data.name: Blog_HAESGC_H4_Text3
data.value: 3. Data Breach Response Plan: In the unfortunate event of a GDPR data breach, having a data breach response plan is essential. AxCrypt can help mitigate the damage by ensuring that encrypted data cannot be accessed or used inappropriately. Having encrypted backups also allows businesses to quickly recover from incidents without compromising sensitive data.

data.name: Blog_HAESGC_H4_Text4
data.value: 4. Cross-Border Data Transfers: When transferring personal data outside of the European Economic Area (EEA), GDPR compliance remains a top priority. AxCrypt supports businesses with secure GDPR compliance, ensuring that personal data remains protected during cross-border transfers. This helps businesses meet GDPR data protection requirements when data is shared internationally.

data.name: Blog_HAESGC_H5_Text1
data.value: Regular Audits and Data Reviews: GDPR compliance is not a one-time effort but an ongoing process. Businesses should conduct regular audits and reviews of their GDPR data protection measures. AxCrypt provides businesses with the features to easily audit and manage encrypted files, ensuring that they remain compliant and protected at all times.

data.name: Blog_HAESGC_H5_Text2
data.value: Staff Training and Awareness: Ensuring that employees are trained on GDPR data security principles is key to maintaining compliance. AxCrypt can be part of an organization’s broader GDPR compliance software training plan, ensuring that employees understand the importance of GDPR encryption in safeguarding personal data.

data.name: Blog_HAESGC_H6_Text1
data.value: Achieving GDPR compliance requires a combination of clear policies, effective practices, and the right tools. AxCrypt’s GDPR encryption features provide businesses with a reliable way to protect sensitive data, adhere to GDPR principles, and avoid the significant penalties associated with GDPR non-compliance.

data.name: Blog_HAESGC_H6_Text2
data.value: By implementing GDPR compliance software like AxCrypt, businesses can ensure that their GDPR data protection strategies align with GDPR’s stringent requirements, safeguarding both customer data and organizational reputation. Start encrypting today to secure your data and build trust with your customers while meeting your GDPR compliance obligations.

data.name: Blog_HDSHTPMDWE_H1_Text1
data.value: Robust data security measures in your healthcare organizations can be a game changer. The security measures will not only prevent sensitive healthcare data from unauthorized access, but they would also ensure continued and streamlined operations, making critical healthcare services readily available without interruptions.

data.name: Blog_HDSHTPMDWE_H1_Text2
data.value: Protecting patient data is not just a legal obligation; it is an ethical imperative. Healthcare providers have a duty to safeguard the sensitive information entrusted to them. HIPAA (Health Insurance Portability and Accountability Act) and other regulations outline strict guidelines for handling and protecting PHI.

data.name: Blog_HDSHTPMDWE_H2_Text1
data.value: A breach containing healthcare data can have detrimental consequences for both the healthcare organizations and the patients. Healthcare has the highest cost of a data breach among all industries, standing at

data.name: Blog_HDSHTPMDWE_H2_Text2
data.value: Identity Theft: Stolen medical records can be used for fraudulent activities, including obtaining medical services, prescription drugs, or loans under a patient's name. This can lead to significant financial losses and emotional distress for patients.

data.name: Blog_HDSHTPMDWE_H2_Text3
data.value: Disruption of Services: Cyberattacks can disrupt healthcare operations, leading to delays in diagnosis, treatments, and appointments. This can have serious consequences for patient care and potentially endanger lives.

data.name: Blog_HDSHTPMDWE_H2_Text4
data.value: Financial Loss: Healthcare organizations can face significant financial losses due to data breaches. This includes fines and penalties for non-compliance with regulations, legal fees, costs associated with notifying patients, and potential reputational damage.

data.name: Blog_HDSHTPMDWE_H2_Text5
data.value: Reputational Damage:Data breaches can erode patient trust and damage the reputation of healthcare providers. This can lead to loss of business, legal repercussions, and difficulty attracting and retaining qualified healthcare professionals.

data.name: Blog_HDSHTPMDWE_H2_Text6
data.value: Discrimination: Sensitive medical information can be used for discrimination in employment, insurance, or other areas of life. This can have a profound impact on a patient's livelihood and well-being.

data.name: Blog_HDSHTPMDWE_H2_Text7
data.value: These devastating consequences highlight the critical need for robust data security measures in the healthcare industry. A proactive data security measure such as file encryption can not only protect sensitive healthcare data from attacks but it will also give healthcare organizations and patients a peace of mind for their data.

data.name: Blog_HDSHTPMDWE_H3_Text1
data.value: File encryption is a process where contents of a file are transformed into an unreadable and undecipherable format. The process involves using an encryption algorithm, such as AES, along with encryption keys. The encryption keys contain the precise pattern for the algorithm to transform the file’s contents, so that the same keys can be used to reverse the encryption process (decryption) to restore the file’s contents to its original state.

data.name: Blog_HDSHTPMDWE_H3_Text2
data.value: File encryption ensures that even if unauthorized individuals gain access to the encrypted healthcare data, they cannot understand or utilize the information, rendering it useless in the hands of cyber attackers.

data.name: Blog_HDSHTPMDWE_H3_Text3
data.value: File encryption is inherently different from other file security measures such as password protection, where files are locked with a layer of password and can easily be broken to gain access to the files.

data.name: Blog_HEIDS_H1_Text1
data.value: Exploitation of an individual’s interest by a scammer in order to access restricted information. Phishing is by far the most entrenched form of data security breach in this sphere. Due to its nature, the victims of this form of data breach at times have no idea that they are leaving themselves open to exploitation. The way phishing works is that the entity with the intention to access unauthorized information lures the potential victim into thinking that they are engaging with a legitimate online entity; usually via email to access the desired information. The victim, unaware that they are being scammed, end up giving the desired information themselves. To the mind of the victim, they are only giving out desired information to a legitimate online platform. The end result is that the person ends up aiding in the data breach, albeit unknowingly, through accessing malicious links or email attachments.

data.name: Blog_HEIDS_H10_Text1
data.value: Outsourcing or dealing with contractors whose perspective of data security might be different from that of the organization that is contacting outside vendors. Outsourcing has been known to contribute to cases of data breaches. When vendors have access to information that is deemed sensitive and they themselves do not appreciate its importance, which could lead to serious data leakages.

data.name: Blog_HEIDS_H2_Text1
data.value: Mail misdelivery is another form of human error that impacts on data security. Misdelivery occurs when those entrusted with the delivery of sensitive information either intentionally or unknowingly end up delivering such information to unauthorized users. In this age of email mass marketing and other forms of massive data transfer, persons handling such transfers are mandated to guarantee the safety of data being sent. The use of encryption in such transfers helps minimize the accessibility of such information should it find its way to unintended recipients.

data.name: Blog_HEIDS_H3_Text1
data.value: Unauthorized access to information outlets such as company devices. Those entrusted with such devices should treat them with the importance they deserve. It’s not uncommon to find employees with access to such devices allowing unrestricted access to their friends or family members. It’s during those interactions that information can be accessed without the person’s knowledge, leading to a serious breach in data security. The owners of such devices should be trained on the importance of the gadgets in their possession as they are literally the gatekeepers of such sensitive information.

data.name: Blog_HEIDS_H4_Text1
data.value: Poor password usage can seriously undermine a person’s or corporate data. The accessibility to such information should be password protected. In fact, it’s no longer just about having a password. More is expected, the routine changing of these passwords guarantees that access to such information is restricted. Another way would be to avoid using obvious words for passwords. Individuals entrusted with password requesting devices should avoid sharing such passwords. Corporations should emphasise to their employees the importance of employing proper password management practices to avoid data security breaches.

data.name: Blog_HEIDS_H5_Text1
data.value: Inadequate or in some cases absence of relevant training on people entrusted with such data. The frequent incorporation of information management systems to members of staff that handle sensitive information minimizes the risk of human error, as members can refer to their training on best practices employed in the handling of such information. The absence of such laid out guidelines and expectations would most definitely expose employees to violations in data security.

data.name: Blog_HEIDS_H6_Text1
data.value: Little awareness of matters relating to data security. Security has to be emphasized to all members handling company data. Issues on software upgrade that bring about improved security measures are not a management issue alone. Best internet and data handling software should be put to use and the relevant persons educated on their importance and use. Things like data security upgrades should be at the forefront of staff members in conjunction with the relevant Information technology personnel. Data security should be a primary responsibility of all staff members; it’s the absence of such awareness that could lead to data being compromised.

data.name: Blog_HEIDS_H7_Text1
data.value: Careless or outright incompetence when it comes to data handling. In the daily execution of one’s duties, set out procedures might be overlooked. The need to meet targets and deadlines will most often make people overlook procedures that they consider cumbersome. These shortcuts are sometimes the root course of known data breaches. It’s the responsibility of those charged with management to ensure laid out data handling procedures adhere to irrespective of the workload. In the rush to finish assignments employees who are not keen to details might be responsible for coursing data breaches.

data.name: Blog_HEIDS_H8_Text1
data.value: Unrestricted data usage is yet another factor that results in data being compromised. The ease with which persons access any or all information should be a subject of scrutiny. By leaving an institution’s data access points manned and the need to apply multiple layers, authentication when accessing or requesting certain data that is considered sensitive is critical in limiting data leakages. The absence of such measures means that anybody with access can retrieve any information they so wish for their personal use. Restriction brings about accountability and traceability, especially when dealing with sensitive information.

data.name: Blog_HEIDS_H9_Text1
data.value: The human aspect associated with budget allocation in matters relating to data security is sometimes to blame for data breaches. With management always on the lookout for cost-cutting measures, the need to invest and come up with a sustained approach to a data breach scenario might not be appreciated. This is especially so when the said company has never experienced any data breaches. The failure to allocate funds and invest in data security measures leaves the company vulnerable to data attacks, more so when they are ill prepared when these attacks occur.

data.name: Blog_HPDYMP_Conclusion_Text1
data.value: Phone encryption is not a new concept in the mobile business, and it has become an unavoidable element of the design process for all smartphone makers. Mobile encryption can accomplish everything for you, from preventing your data from being stolen to keeping your personal information safe. Now that you understand the need for encrypted data, encrypt all of your mobile devices to protect your data from unauthorized access.

data.name: Blog_HPDYMP_H1_Text1
data.value: Mobile phones have become an integral part of our daily lives. They have become the main target for hackers as a result of the global pandemic and the rise in remote work. There are many undiscovered risks out there attempting to get private data on your mobile device. When it comes to the information stored on a phone, many people underestimate its true worth. Your phone contains all of your personal information while acting as a data bank and a social media hub.

data.name: Blog_HPDYMP_H1_Text2
data.value: Mobile security is a precautionary measure used to safeguard data against a variety of threats aimed to invade privacy and steal any other information kept on the phone. These data assaults are aimed towards stealing personal information, such as bank account numbers, login credentials, and other information. Make no mistake about a hacker's abilities. Hackers have a simple way of manipulating or stealing your phone's data. Hacking isn't necessarily limited to collecting usernames and passwords or sending out phishing emails.

data.name: Blog_HPDYMP_H2_Text1
data.value: Identity theft, fraud, and the theft of financial resources from employees and consumers are all possible outcomes of unprotected data. Every year, 4.3% of company-issued smartphones are lost or stolen. On average, roughly 10,573 mobile breaches occur per day. Large, small, public, and private enterprises all experience data breaches. In fact, hackers are increasingly targeting small and mid-sized organizations since their networks are less secure.

data.name: Blog_HPDYMP_H2_Text2
data.value: Hackers now have the ability to listen in on chats and hack into any data on your phone. Without your permission, your social media accounts, bank accounts, sensitive images, private text messages, and more could be accessed.

data.name: Blog_HPDYMP_H3_Text1
data.value: Perhaps the simplest approach to keep your phone safe from unauthorized is using a passcode. But that isn't enough; cracking someone's passcode is no longer rocket science. Mobile data encryption is one of the best ways to protect your sensitive information on a phone, even while you are on the go. AxCrypt Mobile encryption is beyond a regular lock screen password. It is a one-stop for safeguarding all of your personal information and data on your mobile phones from prying eyes. It does so by storing your phone's information in an unreadable, jumbled format that can only be read with the correct credentials. With mobile encryption, you can be certain that your data is protected even if your device is lost or stolen. AxCrypt protects your phone's data using 256-bit AES encryption and other advanced features. You can secure your data on Google Drive Files and Dropbox on your iOS and Android devices with the AxCrypt mobile encryption.

data.value: 'Scientia potentia est' originating from Latin, meaning knowledge is power, is a relevant aphorism that can be associated with today's world. This dictum is now truer than ever, as a result of rapid advances in information technology.

data.name: Blog_HPYBFC_H1_Text2
data.value: Furthermore, we want to continue ensuring and raising awareness around encryption and cyber security, and therefore we are glad to share some information on how to protect yourself and your business from cyber threats.

data.name: Blog_HPYBFC_H2_Text1
data.value: In simple terms, a cyber attack is an assault launched by cybercriminals using one or more computers against a single or multiple computers or networks. A cyber attack can maliciously disable computers, steal data, or use a breached computer as a launch point for other attacks in order to expose, alter, disable, destroy, steal or gain information through unauthorized access to or make unauthorized use of an asset. A cyberattack may steal, alter, or destroy a specified target by hacking into a susceptible system. Cybercriminals use a variety of methods to launch a cyber attack, including malware, phishing, ransomware, denial of service, among other methods.

data.name: Blog_HPYBFC_H3_Text1
data.value: • Malware

data.name: Blog_HPYBFC_H3_Text2

data.name: Blog_HPYBFC_H3_Text3

data.name: Blog_HPYBFC_H3_Text6

data.name: Blog_HPYBFC_H3_Text7
data.value: • SQL injection

data.name: Blog_HPYBFC_H3_Text8
data.value: • Zero-day exploits

data.name: Blog_HPYBFC_H4_Text1
data.value: A cyberattack occurs when cybercriminals try to gain illegal access to electronic data stored on a computer or a network. The intent might be to inflict reputational damage or harm to a business or person, or theft of valuable data. Cyberattacks can target individuals, groups, organizations, or governments.

data.name: Blog_HPYBFC_H4_Text2
data.value: A data breach is a type of security incident. It occurs when information is accessed without authorization. The information accessed could include personal information such as Social Security numbers, passwords, and financial account numbers.

data.name: Blog_HPYBFC_H5_SH1_Text1
data.value: Using strong passwords is one way to protect your information online, so avoid using the same, easy-to-crack passwords, no matter how much you love your pet. Adopt symbols, numbers and different figures so no one can guess it by knowing personal information about you. You can also use the AxCrypt Password Generator that produces strong passwords that are not nonsensical and actually possible to remember and type. You'll get three suggestions of decreasing strength and complexity.

data.name: Blog_HPYBFC_H5_SH2_Text1
data.value: Encryption is a way to make communications that are intended to be private actually remain private. It will help protect customers' data and anticipate threats. By encrypting your data and making it unreadable you guarantee security and productivity. Even if intercepted, the message will be unreadable for any actor that doesn't possess the right key to decrypt it.

data.name: Blog_HPYBFC_H5_SH3_Text1
data.value: Backing up your business's data and website will help you recover any information you lose if you experience a cyber incident or have computer issues. It's essential that you backup your most important data and information regularly.

data.name: Blog_HPYBFC_H5_SH3_Text2
data.value: Ensure you use multi-factor authentication (MFA). MFA is a verification security process that requires you to provide two or more proofs of your identity before you can access your account. For example, a system will require a password and a code sent to your mobile device before access is granted. Multi-factor authentication adds an additional layer of security to make it harder for attackers to gain access to your device or online accounts.

data.name: Blog_HPYBFC_H5_SH4_Text1
data.value: Train every new employee to protect valuable data and have them sign your information policy. Use newsletters and/or ongoing training to reinforce your culture of cybersecurity. Raise cyber security awareness among the staff and teach them how to access data in the best, secure way on every device. They should know the risks of using data with an unsecure network. That can save the company from a massive loss in the years to come. Your business is only as secure as its weakest link.

data.name: Blog_HQHCYP_H1_Text1
data.value: Before we dive deeper into details of password authentication and password cracking methods, let’s first look at some stats and understand how they impact the way you generate, use, and save new passwords.

data.name: Blog_HQHCYP_H1_Text10
data.value: 9.Over 80% of users admit to reusing passwords across multiple accounts.

data.name: Blog_HQHCYP_H1_Text11
data.value: 10.In 2022, there were over 2.29 billion global records exposed in data breaches.

data.name: Blog_HQHCYP_H1_Text12
data.value: 11.Phishing is the most common tactic used by hackers to obtain passwords.

data.name: Blog_HQHCYP_H1_Text13
data.value: 12.Brute force attacks are responsible for approximately 5% of successful data breaches. Brute force attack is a trial-and-error method used by hackers to guess a password by systematically checking all possible combinations of characters until the correct one is found. The checking is done using automated tools or a coding script written by hackers.

data.name: Blog_HQHCYP_H1_Text2
data.value: 1.In 2022,“123456” was the most commonly used password, followed by “123456789” and “password”.

data.name: Blog_HQHCYP_H1_Text3
data.value: 2.A recent survey showed that only 53% of people use different passwords for different accounts, leaving the rest vulnerable to potential hacks.

data.name: Blog_HQHCYP_H1_Text4
data.value: 3.The average user has 26 password protected accounts.

data.name: Blog_HQHCYP_H1_Text5
data.value: 4.Approximately 10% of internet users have used “123456” as their password.

data.name: Blog_HQHCYP_H1_Text6
data.value: 5.A six-character password containing only lowercase letters can be cracked in less than 10 minutes.

data.name: Blog_HQHCYP_H1_Text7
data.value: 6.A 12-character password containing uppercase letters, lowercase letters, numbers, and symbols can take over 1,000 years to crack.

data.name: Blog_HQHCYP_H1_Text8
data.value: 7.The most common password length is 8 characters.

data.name: Blog_HQHCYP_H1_Text9
data.value: 8.Approximately 81% of data breaches are due to weak or stolen passwords.

data.name: Blog_HQHCYP_H2_Text1
data.value: When you log in to a website or application, the password authentication process begins. You enter your username or email address and password, and the website or app checks this information against a database of user credentials.

data.name: Blog_HQHCYP_H2_Text2
data.value: The password you enter is usually encrypted using a mathematical algorithm, such as SHA-256 or AES-256, which scrambles your password into a unique string of characters that cannot be easily reversed or deciphered. This encrypted version of your password is stored in the website or app's database, along with your username or email address.

data.name: Blog_HQHCYP_H2_Text3
data.value: During the account creation process, the password is first hashed (converted) using a one-way function that transforms the password into a unique string of characters. The resulting hash is then stored in the system's database. The next time the user tries to log in, the password they provide is hashed again and compared to the stored hash. If the two hashes match, the user is authenticated and granted access to the system.

data.name: Blog_HQHCYP_H2_Text4
data.value: To ensure the security of the password, it is essential to hash the password before storing it in the system's database. Hashing ensures that the password is not saved in plain text, making it difficult for attackers to read and use the password if they gain access to the system's database.

data.name: Blog_HQHCYP_H2_Text5
data.value: Moreover, many systems incorporate additional security measures like salting, which adds a random string of characters to the password before hashing. Salting ensures that attackers cannot use precomputed hashes of commonly used passwords to easily crack the password, adding another layer of security.

data.name: Blog_HQHCYP_H2_Text6
data.value: When you try to log in again, the website or app will re-encrypt the password you enter and compare it to the encrypted version stored in the database. If the two versions match, you are granted access to the site or app. This process ensures that only authorized users with the correct password can access their accounts.

data.name: Blog_HQHCYP_H2_Text7
data.value: Password authentication is not always fool proof. Passwords can be stolen or guessed by attackers using various methods, such as brute-force attacks or social engineering. As a result, it is essential to follow password best practices, such as using a long and complex password, using unique passwords for each account, and changing passwords frequently.

data.name: Blog_HQHCYP_H3_Text1
data.value: Hackers use various methods and algorithms to crack passwords, including brute force attacks and social engineering techniques like phishing. Let’s explore some of the most commonly used techniques for password cracking.

data.name: Blog_HQHCYP_H3_Text2
data.value: Brute Force Attack: The most basic algorithm of cracking a password is known as a brute force attack. This method involves using a program to guess every possible combination of characters until the correct password is found. While this may seem like a time-consuming and tedious process, modern computers are incredibly fast and can guess millions of password combinations per second.

data.name: Blog_HQHCYP_H3_Text3
data.value: Dictionary Attack: Another method used to crack passwords is the dictionary attack. In this method, the attacker uses a program that has a pre-existing list of commonly used passwords and tries them one by one until the correct password is found. This list of passwords is known as a password dictionary and can be created by the attacker or downloaded from the internet.

data.name: Blog_HQHCYP_H3_Text4
data.value: Phishing: Phishing is a social engineering attack that involves tricking a user into revealing their password. Attackers create fake login pages that look identical to the real ones and send the user a link to the fake page. When the user enters their password, the attacker captures it and can use it to gain access to the user's account.

data.name: Blog_HQHCYP_H3_Text5
data.value: Keystroke Logging: Keystroke logging involves installing a program on a victim's computer that records every keystroke made by the user, including their password. Attackers can then retrieve the recorded keystrokes and use them to gain access to the victim's account.

data.name: Blog_HQHCYP_H3_Text6
data.value: Shoulder Surfing: Shoulder surfing involves physically watching a user enter their password. Attackers can do this by standing close to the victim or using a hidden camera to record the user's keystrokes. Once the password is captured, the attacker can use it to gain access to the user's account.

data.name: Blog_HQHCYP_H3_Text7
data.value: Each technique has its own strengths and weaknesses, and hackers very cleverly utilize each of it to prepare and execute the attack. As a result, it is crucial to have a comprehensive approach to password protection to ensure that your credentials are secure from hacking attempt

data.name: Blog_HQHCYP_H4_Text1
data.value: To ensure the security of your passwords and protect them from malicious attacks by hackers, there are several methods, tips, and best practices that can be employed. By implementing the appropriate methods and techniques, you can ensure that your passwords remain safe and secure at all times. Some of the best methods you can use are:

data.name: Blog_HQHCYP_H4_Text2
data.value: Complex Passwords: One of the simplest ways to protect your passwords is to use strong and complex passwords. Passwords should be at least eight characters long and should include a combination of uppercase and lowercase letters, numbers, and symbols. A strong password makes it more difficult for hackers to crack your password using brute-force attacks.

data.name: Blog_HQHCYP_H4_Text3
data.value: For example, a password like “X@xg0n$&p1E” would take billions of years to be cracked using brute force even with the fastest computers available today. You can use a password generator like AxCrypt’s Password Manager to automatically generate and save complex passwords.

data.name: Blog_HQHCYP_H4_Text4
data.value: Password Managers: A password manager is a tool that generates and stores complex passwords for all your online accounts. It stores your passwords in an encrypted database, and you only need to remember one master password to access all your passwords. This method of password protection helps to ensure that you don't use the same password for multiple accounts, which reduces the risk of a password breach.

data.name: Blog_HQHCYP_H4_Text5
data.value: Two-Factor Authentication (2FA): Two-factor authentication adds an extra layer of security to your account. It requires you to enter a verification code in addition to your password to log into your account. The verification code can be sent to your phone via text message, email, or an authenticator app. This method of authentication helps to ensure that only the authorized user has access to the account.

data.name: Blog_HQHCYP_H4_Text6
data.value: Biometric Authentication: Biometric authentication uses unique biological characteristics such as fingerprints, facial recognition, or iris scans to identify users. This method of authentication is more secure than passwords since it's difficult for hackers to fake biometric data. Biometric authentication is increasingly being used in mobile devices and laptops to improve security.

data.name: Blog_HQHCYP_H4_Text7
data.value: Password-less Authentication: Password-less authentication is a new trend in password protection. It replaces the traditional password with other forms of authentication such as biometrics, security tokens, or one-time passwords.

data.name: Blog_HQHCYP_H4_Text8
data.value: This method of authentication is more secure since it eliminates the risk of password theft and password reuse.

data.name: Blog_HQHCYP_H4_Text9
data.value: Apart from these methods, one more highly effective password protection practice is to change your password frequently. This is because the longer you use a password, the higher the chances are that it may get compromised. Regularly changing your password ensures that even if a hacker gains access to it, they won't be able to use it for long before it becomes invalid.

data.name: Blog_HQHCYP_H5_Text1
data.value: A password manager is a software application that helps users generate, store, and manage passwords securely. It’s a tool that can be used to create unique, complex passwords for each of your online accounts and store them in a secure vault. The benefits of using a password manager are numerous, but the primary advantage is that it makes it easier to create and remember strong passwords.

data.name: Blog_HQHCYP_H5_Text2
data.value: Using a password manager can also improve the overall security of your online accounts. Since many people tend to use the same password across multiple accounts, if one password is compromised, it can lead to a domino effect of security breaches across all your other accounts. With a password manager, you can ensure that each account has a unique and complex password, which greatly reduces the risk of a data breach.

data.name: Blog_HQHCYP_H5_Text3
data.value: Another advantage of using a password manager is that it can save you a lot of time. Remembering multiple passwords can be difficult, and having to reset them frequently can be frustrating. With a password manager, you only need to remember one master password to access all of your other passwords. This not only saves you time, but it also reduces the chances of forgetting your password and being locked out of your account.

data.name: Blog_HQHCYP_H5_Text4
data.value: Opting for a password manager is a wise decision that can provide you with peace of mind. With its simple yet effective approach, you can secure your online accounts and steer clear of the stress and financial loss that often accompany data breaches. By taking proactive measures to safeguard your personal information, you can rest assured that your online accounts are well protected, and your sensitive data is safe from prying eyes.

Additionally, AxCrypt's password generator feature can help you create complex and unique passwords for each of your online accounts, making it more difficult for hackers to gain access to your personal data.

This means that you can access your saved passwords and login information across multiple devices, making it more convenient to manage your online accounts. Whether you're on your computer or your phone, you can easily retrieve your login information without having to remember all of your passwords.

data.value: AxCrypt’s password manager is a great choice for those who prioritize security and convenience. With its advanced encryption, password generator, and credential syncing features, you can feel confident that your online accounts are well-protected from potential cyber-attacks.
